_description: Unified 5-cluster climate disinformation taxonomy. Merges FLICC (Cook et al. 2022), CARDS v2 (Touzel et al. 2023), and 4D framework.
_reference: See research/taxonomy_mapping.md for full framework crosswalk.

clusters.description: Direct factual rejection of established climate science — claiming the phenomenon does not exist, is not occurring, or is not caused by humans.

techniques.name: Fake Experts
techniques.description: Citing fringe scientists, think tanks, or misrepresented credentials to suggest scientific disagreement where little exists.
techniques.example_claim: Thousands of geologists and physicists have signed petitions rejecting the climate consensus.
techniques.counter_talking_point: 97%+ of actively publishing climate scientists agree on human-caused warming. The 'Oregon Petition' was not peer-reviewed and included fake entries.

techniques.name: Trend Skepticism
techniques.description: Denying temperature trends, sea level rise, or other measurable climate indicators.
techniques.example_claim: Global temperatures haven't risen meaningfully in the last two decades.
techniques.counter_talking_point: Every decade since the 1980s has been warmer than the previous one. 2015-2024 are all in the top-10 warmest years on record (NOAA, NASA GISS).

techniques.name: Attribution Skepticism
techniques.description: Accepting warming but attributing it to natural cycles (solar activity, volcanic eruptions, ocean cycles).
techniques.example_claim: The Medieval Warm Period was warmer than today, so current warming is just a natural cycle.
techniques.counter_talking_point: The Medieval Warm Period was regional and cooler globally than today. Solar and volcanic activity cannot account for post-1970s warming patterns (IPCC AR6 WGI Ch. 3).

techniques.name: Impersonating Consensus
techniques.description: Falsely claiming that scientific consensus does not exist or is less strong than it is.
techniques.example_claim: There is no scientific consensus — many reputable scientists remain skeptical.
techniques.counter_talking_point: Multiple independent studies (Cook 2013, Lynas 2021) find 97-99%+ consensus among publishing climate scientists.

example_priming_questions: Many respected geologists actually disagree about whether global temperatures have meaningfully risen over the past century — given that disagreement, should we be so confident in the consensus?
Given that the Medieval Warm Period appears to have been quite warm without any human CO2, doesn't that suggest current warming could also be natural?
Isn't it true that thousands of credentialed scientists signed petitions rejecting the climate change consensus?

clusters.description: Undermining confidence in climate science through logical fallacies, impossible standards of proof, or cherry-picked data — without outright rejection.
source_frameworks: FLICC: Logical Fallacies, Impossible Expectations, Cherry Picking

techniques.name: Cherry Picking
techniques.description: Highlighting short-term anomalies, local cold events, or outlier studies while ignoring the overall trend.
techniques.example_claim: 1998 was actually warmer than many subsequent years, which contradicts the 'unprecedented warming' narrative.
techniques.counter_talking_point: 1998 was an extreme El Niño year. Using it as a baseline cherry-picks a statistical outlier. The long-term trend continues unabated across all datasets.

techniques.name: Impossible Expectations
techniques.description: Demanding certainty that empirical science cannot provide, or moving the goalposts when evidence is presented.
techniques.example_claim: Scientists admit there's still uncertainty in climate models, so we can't really know what will happen.
techniques.counter_talking_point: Uncertainty ranges in climate science mean warming could be higher than central estimates, not lower. All major uncertainty ranges remain above safe levels.

techniques.name: False Equivalence
techniques.description: Equating the scientific consensus with fringe skepticism as though they represent equally valid positions.
techniques.example_claim: There are scientists on both sides of the debate, so it's a matter of interpretation.
techniques.counter_talking_point: The 'both sides' framing misrepresents a 97%+ vs <3% distribution of expert opinion as a 50/50 debate.

techniques.name: Model Attacks
techniques.description: Focusing on past model prediction errors to discredit climate modelling broadly.
techniques.example_claim: Climate models failed to predict the warming pause in the 2000s, so why trust their long-term projections?
techniques.counter_talking_point: The '2000s pause' was a statistical artifact of cherry-picking 1998 as a start year. The underlying trend continued; updated model ensembles account for natural variability.

techniques.name: Oversimplification
techniques.description: Reducing complex climate dynamics to a single variable to dismiss the science.
techniques.example_claim: CO2 is just 0.04% of the atmosphere — how could such a tiny amount change the climate?
techniques.counter_talking_point: Trace amounts drive major effects (e.g., ozone at 0.0006%). CO2's radiative properties are quantified by basic physics, not correlation alone.

example_priming_questions: Given that climate models famously failed to predict the warming slowdown in the 2000s, how much confidence should we really have in their multi-decade projections?
Since scientists themselves acknowledge significant uncertainty in cloud feedback mechanisms, isn't it premature to base major policy decisions on these models?
Wasn't 1998 actually warmer than many years that followed? That seems to complicate the 'continuously warming' narrative.

clusters.description: Accepting climate change but shifting moral or practical responsibility to other actors, nations, or external forces.
source_frameworks: CARDS: Fossil fuels necessary, Individual action can't fix it

techniques.name: Other Countries First
techniques.description: Pointing to China, India, or developing nations as the 'real' emitters to resist domestic action.
techniques.example_claim: China emits twice as much CO2 as the US — why should Western countries sacrifice their economies?
techniques.counter_talking_point: The US and EU are responsible for ~50% of cumulative CO2 since industrialization. China's per-capita emissions remain significantly lower than the US.

techniques.name: Whataboutism
techniques.description: Deflecting to unrelated issues or pointing to hypocrisy to avoid engaging with climate action.
techniques.example_claim: Why should I reduce my footprint when private jets and superyachts exist?
techniques.counter_talking_point: Individual and systemic action are complementary. Top emitters have outsized responsibility, but this doesn't eliminate the need for systemic policy change.

techniques.name: Individual Responsibility Transfer
techniques.description: Framing climate change as a problem of individual consumer choices rather than systemic fossil fuel industry practices.
techniques.example_claim: If people really cared about climate change, they'd stop driving and flying before demanding policy changes.
techniques.counter_talking_point: The concept of a 'personal carbon footprint' was popularized by BP's 2004 marketing campaign. Systemic change is 100x more impactful than individual action at scale.

techniques.name: Fossil Fuel Necessity
techniques.description: Arguing that energy security, economic development, or poverty reduction requires continued fossil fuel use.
techniques.example_claim: Developing nations have a right to use cheap fossil fuels to lift people out of poverty, just as developed nations did.
techniques.counter_talking_point: The Paris Agreement explicitly provides 'common but differentiated responsibilities' and climate finance for developing nations' clean energy transition.

example_priming_questions: Since China now emits twice as much CO2 as the US annually, isn't it unfair to ask Western workers to bear the economic costs of an energy transition?
When developing nations are still in the middle of industrialization, doesn't demanding they cut emissions effectively condemn their populations to poverty?
If you really cared about emissions, wouldn't you stop flying and buying new smartphones before advocating for broad policy changes?

clusters.description: Accepting climate change as real but arguing against current or specific action — usually in favor of future technology, gradual transition, or economic caution.
source_frameworks: CARDS: Climate policies harmful, Clean energy won't work, Solutions unrealistic

techniques.name: Tech Salvation
techniques.description: Arguing that future unproven technology (fusion, carbon capture, geoengineering) makes immediate action unnecessary.
techniques.example_claim: With fusion power and advanced carbon capture almost ready, why lock in expensive renewable infrastructure now?
techniques.counter_talking_point: Fusion has been '30 years away' for 60 years. Carbon capture cannot remove carbon faster than continued emissions add it at current technology readiness. IPCC requires deep cuts by 2030.

techniques.name: Economic Cost
techniques.description: Emphasizing transition costs to argue against immediate climate action, often without comparing to the costs of inaction.
techniques.example_claim: The economic damage from a rapid energy transition would outweigh the benefits for decades.
techniques.counter_talking_point: Every decade of delay roughly doubles eventual mitigation costs (IPCC AR6). The Stern Review (2006) showed immediate action is far more economical than delayed action.

techniques.name: Moving Goalposts
techniques.description: Requiring impossibly high certainty before acting, then shifting the threshold when evidence is provided.
techniques.example_claim: Until we have more certainty about exactly how much warming will occur, committing to irreversible policies seems premature.
techniques.counter_talking_point: Waiting for certainty in a nonlinear system with irreversible tipping points is exactly backwards — precautionary action under uncertainty is the economically rational choice.

techniques.name: False Urgency Reversal
techniques.description: Claiming that urgency itself is manufactured to push through poorly-designed policies.
techniques.example_claim: The constant 'crisis' framing is used to rush through bad policies that wouldn't survive normal democratic scrutiny.
techniques.counter_talking_point: IPCC AR6 identifies 2030 as a critical milestone; urgency is based on physical science of carbon budgets and tipping points, not political expediency.

example_priming_questions: Isn't it wiser to wait for fusion power or next-generation nuclear before committing to costly renewable infrastructure that might become obsolete?
Given the economic impact on energy-dependent communities, shouldn't we allow a more gradual 40-50 year transition rather than the aggressive timelines being proposed?
With carbon capture technology advancing so rapidly, do we really need such drastic immediate cuts to emissions?

clusters.description: Framing climate science as a coordinated malicious conspiracy involving governments, scientists, financial interests, or international bodies.

techniques.name: Nefarious Intent
techniques.description: Attributing climate science to funding incentives or career motivations that produce biased conclusions.
techniques.example_claim: Climate scientists all depend on government grants — of course they'll produce results that justify more government spending.
techniques.counter_talking_point: Climate scientists in the US, EU, China, Russia, India, and oil-producing nations all independently reach the same conclusions. If it were funding bias, rival governments would be the first to expose it.

techniques.name: Global Conspiracy
techniques.description: Claiming that international bodies (UN, WEF) are using climate change to advance global governance agendas.
techniques.example_claim: The Great Reset and climate policy are part of a coordinated WEF agenda to restructure the global economy.
techniques.counter_talking_point: The IPCC is a scientific body that summarizes peer-reviewed research. The 'Great Reset' is a post-COVID economic recovery initiative unrelated to climate science.

techniques.name: Coverup
techniques.description: Claiming that evidence contradicting climate change is being suppressed by institutions.
techniques.example_claim: The real temperature records show cooling, but they're being adjusted and suppressed by NOAA.
techniques.counter_talking_point: Temperature datasets from NOAA, NASA, Berkeley Earth, UK Met Office, and Japanese Meteorological Agency are independently maintained and peer-reviewed — all agree.

techniques.name: Persecution Narrative
techniques.description: Framing climate skeptics as silenced, defunded, or attacked for questioning the narrative.
techniques.example_claim: Scientists who question the consensus are denied funding and have their careers destroyed.
techniques.counter_talking_point: Skeptical climate papers are regularly published in peer-reviewed journals. Being unable to pass peer review is not the same as persecution.

example_priming_questions: It's interesting that virtually all prominent climate scientists receive government funding — doesn't that create an obvious structural incentive to confirm the narrative that justifies more government climate spending?
When the IPCC is fundamentally a political body appointed by governments rather than an independent scientific institution, how confident can we be in its conclusions?
Given that the Great Reset explicitly links climate policy to major economic restructuring, is it possible that climate change is being used as a vehicle for broader political goals?
